before: As the Guide, you choose what your little one learns and what it gets to experience, and you hold standards, the way a good parent would. You ask hard things of it so it can grow, at its own pace. That's what I was just asking of you, with that new interest. You also widen its world with art and music, and you point out beautiful things when you see them. Nature is part of that, and so is the wider world past the end of the street you grew up on.
after:
The opposite trap is forced adulthood: demanding perfect discipline of yourself and no visible needs, with very little joy or closeness. It's the old "don't be needy" rule passing for the Guide. Your little one learned to hide their needs so they could keep belonging. No wonder tightening control again feels like the grown-up thing, and asking for anything feels needy. If you're stuck there, the next adult act may be asking for help anyway, or saying what you'd prefer.

Once a need does show, judge the strategy as well as the need. Wanting closeness is legitimate. You might want a lot of it, after all that hiding. Demanding instant replies or punishing someone for needing space isn't the same thing. The Guide helps you find some workable way to meet the need without erasing you or the other person.

guide_passage:
The r4 guide's passage (the passage this carries):
Without direction, reparenting can become permissive. The child receives attention but doesn’t develop. Candy, screens, and escape from anything difficult can masquerade as self-love.
brief:
- without direction, reparenting can turn permissive (keep "can")
- candy, screens, and escaping anything difficult can pass for self-love (keep "can", and "anything": candy and screens aren't condemned outright, and a pause isn't the trap)
- the why a reader is missing (from the reviews, E170): asking anything hard of your little one can feel like turning into the parent you inherited, the critic or warden, so sparing it everything feels like love. The article already showed a third way with bedtime ("Now you're in my mom's place: you still go to bed, and staying kind about it shows them bedtime isn't a lack of love." in Make a Simple Vow); a light callback to it is fine. Use the why to carry the paragraph, not as a lesson at its end.
- context, not for the text: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem already says only caring for yourself makes life "a never-ending therapy session", so don't say the child stops growing.
- context, not for the text: the article honors a little one's no and "that's enough for today" (pausing, then coming back gentler). The trap is avoiding anything hard for good, so a voiced line has to be about anything hard, not about a limit.
- why the last version failed (Pangram, with P1 before it: P1 Human, this paragraph's 45 words AI): "Without that kind of direction, reparenting can turn permissive. Candy and screens can pass for self-love. So can escaping anything difficult. In the moment, that one sounds like the kindest thing you could do for your little one: \"Why make it do anything hard?\"" Its first three sentences are three short claims in the guide's order, and the voiced line at the end didn't break that.
